title: The mobile visit for a small clinic
metaTitle: A small clinic mobile website that can book
excerpt: Most patients will judge a small clinic on a phone. The first screen still has to show the room, the clinician, and a way to book a visit.
alt: A white wall covered with framed prints, small plants, and two floating shelves, a narrow wall arranged so each object stays readable, for a phone screen that has to stay just as clear.
caption: Prints, plants, and two shelves on a white wall. A phone screen should be this uncrowded. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should the first phone screen of a clinic site show?
faqs.answer: The room or the clinician, a sentence about the visit, and a way to book or call. Hours or the neighborhood can fit if they are one line. A procedure list, a stock smile, and a welcome essay do not belong in that first view. Patients decide from the screen they can see without scrolling.

faqs.question: Should the phone number be on the mobile homepage?
faqs.answer: Yes. Make it text a thumb can tap, next to the booking button, with hours nearby. Many anxious patients would rather call than use a form. A number that only appears in the footer, or only as an icon, will be missed by the people who needed it most.

faqs.question: How fast should the clinic page load on a phone?
faqs.answer: web.dev's Core Web Vitals guidance says a good Largest Contentful Paint is within 2.5 seconds, a good Interaction to Next Paint is 200 milliseconds or less, and a good Cumulative Layout Shift is 0.1 or less, at the 75th percentile of visits. On a clinic page those targets keep the room and the booking from arriving late or jumping under a thumb.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A small clinic mobile website is the visit most patients will have. They are on a phone, often away from a desk, sometimes already uncomfortable. The first screen still has to show the room, the clinician, and a way to book a visit.

Do not let the desktop composition decide that screen. A wide photograph of the building, a long welcome, and a button below the fold is a brochure. The phone page is the front door.

## Design the column before the billboard

Open the layout at phone width first. You have a narrow stack and a short first view, partly eaten by the browser and by a map pin they might have tapped. Into what remains, put a recognizable room or face, one sentence, and a booking. If those do not fit, do not move on to a desktop version that hides the problem with whitespace.

Nielsen Norman Group's research gives the time budget. People often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and the value has to be clear in about 10 seconds if you want them to stay. On a phone outside a clinic, or in a kitchen after the children are in bed, those seconds include glare and one free hand. There is no room for a slider.

The sentence should wrap in two lines. "First visits for joint pain with Dr. Shah. Book or call." Add the street in the next line if you can. A six-line headline about compassionate care pushes the room and the button down into the territory people do not reach. Write the short line before anyone chooses a typeface.

Sticky booking is useful when it is one control and it does not cover the phone number or the picture of the room. A sticky bar plus a chat bubble plus a cookie banner is a crowd on a small screen. Pick the booking. Let the cookie sit in a single line. Retire the chat on the marketing page if it fights the button.

## The first screen, in the order of arrival

Stack the decision the way a patient rehearses it.

1. Who the visit is for, in their words.
2. The room or the clinician, large enough to recognize.
3. A line on access or hours if that is what stops people.
4. Book a visit, and the phone number beside or under it.

The picture has to survive the width. A doorway with the step visible. A face that is still a face. If the only honest photo becomes a blur, use a tighter crop and put the access fact in type. "Two steps at the door. Ring the bell." Type is more reliable than a tiny detail in a compressed image.

Do not autoplay a film of the renovation. Patients did not come for the renovation. If you have a short clip of the room, leave it behind the first still, with a control, and honor reduced motion. The still must be enough.

Logo rows of insurers and associations go below the booking, or they go away. On a phone they are a fence between the patient and the action. A single line, "Bring your insurance card and we will confirm before the visit," does more than eight tiny marks.

## Calm that still fits

An anxious patient looks for specifics, not a softer font. The mobile page can be calm by being short. Name the clinician. Say the first visit does not include a procedure, if that is true. Say how long it usually takes. These are one-line reassurances. A paragraph about your philosophy will be skipped, and the skip will feel like the answers were withheld.

Put the fee shape within the first scroll. Not the whole tariff. The first-visit number, or a plain statement that the desk quotes it before you come, if you truly cannot publish it. Hiding a knowable fee below a long story makes the phone page feel slippery. Slippery is the wrong texture here.

Address and hours must be text, not a picture of a business card. Text can be tapped, copied, and read aloud by a screen reader. A map can follow. The sentence comes first. "George Street. Two steps. Open Tuesday to Friday, 8 to 4." A patient in a car can use that. They cannot pinch a watercolor map.

Stock smiles are worse on a phone because they fill the only frame you had. If you do not have a photo of the room yet, use type and book the shoot. Do not rent a face to fill the hero. A blank, honest layout is a better preview than a false one.

## Booking with a thumb

The booking control should name the visit and open the right appointment type. A patient should not have to choose "department" after they already tapped "Book a first visit." If your widget cannot accept that, the widget is part of the design problem, not a separate IT problem.

Ask for the minimum. Name, phone, the reason in their words. Insurance and history can be a later step, or a clipboard in the room, unless you truly cannot hold the slot without them. Say which, on the button's line. "We will ask for a phone number and the reason. The fee is confirmed by the desk." Surprise fields are how half-finished bookings happen.

Errors sit next to the field in words. Do not clear the form. Do not rely on a red outline. The keyboard will cover the bottom of the screen. Keep the focused field in view. These are ordinary build tasks, and they are the difference between a booked visit and a patient who thinks the clinic is closed.

Offer the call as a peer. Tap-to-call with the number visible. Hours visible. If nobody will answer, say when someone will. A phone that rings out is a mobile experience too. The page should not promise a voice you do not staff.

## Speed and a page that does not jump

web.dev defines three Core Web Vitals that apply to this screen. Largest Contentful Paint should occur within 2.5 seconds for a good loading experience. Interaction to Next Paint should be 200 milliseconds or less, so a tap on Book registers. Cumulative Layout Shift should stay at 0.1 or less, so the button does not move as fonts and banners arrive. Judge them at the 75th percentile of real visits, not on the office wifi alone.

On a clinic homepage the largest element is usually the room photograph. Send a phone-sized file, not a desktop original. Crop before you compress. A tighter, truer picture is often the faster one. INP suffers when the booking widget loads a large script before it can be tapped. Load what the first tap needs. CLS suffers when a consent bar or a chat bubble pushes the number down after the patient has aimed. Reserve the space, or do not inject the bar late.

Hanabi builds this kind of site in Next.js, with React, TypeScript, and Tailwind, hosted on Vercel. The point of naming the stack is ownership and weight. The clinic should be able to change an hour or a fee without a new photoshoot, and the phone page should not wait on a page builder's leftover scripts. Motion, if any, should not be what blows the loading budget. Reduced motion stays on.

Test on a mid-range phone on an ordinary street, which is where your patients are. If the room image is slow, it is the wrong file. If the button jumps, it is not finished, no matter how the desktop looks in the studio.

## Editing a desktop design down

If a wide layout already exists, cut it rather than shrinking it.

- One sentence, not a welcome and a sub-welcome.
- The room or the face, not a collage.
- Booking and phone above the procedure list.
- Procedure list removed from the first screen entirely.
- Header reduced to wordmark, book, and call.
- Video and sliders deleted.

Then check the page in a real mobile browser. Preview frames lie about chrome, font size, and the consent bar. Those pixels belong to the patient. Read the first screen aloud in sunlight. If you cannot see the clinician's face or the booking, the contrast or the crop is wrong. Fix it before you discuss a second type style.

Landscape does not need its own story. The booking and the phone should remain reachable if someone turns the device. That is the whole extra requirement.

[Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) is a set of public sites edited down to a legible first view. Use that as a comparison when a desktop frame is arguing for one more line. The phone does not have the line to spare.

## Walk the visit with someone else

Hand your phone to a person who has booked care while worried. Ask them what the place is, who they would see, and how they would book or call. Watch the thumb. If they scroll immediately, the order is wrong. If they pinch, the proof is too small. If they tap and nothing they understand happens, the widget is wrong.

Do the same with the address. Can they start directions without copying a number out of a picture? Can they tell about the steps before they leave home? Those are mobile tasks. A beautiful desktop waiting room does not complete them.

When the first screen works, the remaining risk is the path after the tap. [A contact path for a small clinic](/blog/a-contact-path-for-a-small-clinic) covers what the patient hears next, how fast the desk confirms, and how to keep the form from becoming a second waiting room.
